sections.overview: The spotted wobbegong is a flattened carpet shark of the coastal waters of southern and eastern Australia. It spends the day motionless on the bottom and hunts at night, relying on camouflage and ambush rather than speed.
sections.identification: The head is flat and fringed on each side with 6–10 branched, fleshy lobes. The body is yellowish to greenish-brown with large dark saddles and whitish O-shaped rings, and there are two dorsal fins but no fin spines. Most adults measure 150–180 cm, though the maximum is cited as about 320 cm, and newborns are about 21–23 cm. The consulted species references do not provide a reliable adult body mass for identification; no weight is estimated here.
sections.habitat: It lives on the continental shelf from the intertidal zone to about 218 m, mostly in shallow water, on rocky and coral reefs, sand, seagrass beds and under piers. Its range runs from Queensland around southern Australia to Western Australia; records from Japan and the South China Sea are probably misidentifications.
sections.diet: It eats bottom invertebrates such as crabs, lobsters and octopuses, and bony fishes including sea basses, scorpionfishes and luderick. Smaller sharks are also taken. It catches prey by sucking it in with a sudden opening of the jaws.
sections.behavior: It is sluggish and often rests on the sea floor for long periods, mostly in daytime. The fringe of lobes around its head breaks up its outline and acts as a lure, and prey sometimes nibble it before being seized. It looks docile but can bite hard if provoked or stepped on, and often does not let go.
sections.reproduction: It is ovoviviparous: the eggs develop inside the female, and the young are born independent. Litters reach up to 37 pups after a gestation of 10–11 months, with births in spring. Females have a cycle of about three years, and males hold a female by biting near her gills during mating.
sections.ecology: As a nocturnal ambush predator with a trophic level of about 4.2, it feeds on both invertebrates and fishes of reefs and sand. It carries many parasites, including 33 species of tapeworm reported in one account.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists it as Least Concern (assessed 2015, as reported by FishBase). It is caught as bycatch in trawls and lobster pots and by spearfishing. In New South Wales, trawling caused declines in the early 1990s and the species was listed as Vulnerable there; numbers later stabilised, and bag and size limits now apply to recreational fishing.
